6. The transport process or mechanism of GlyT2 need to be investigated in detail so that the
inhibitory effect upon RPI-GLYT2-82 and ORG25543 binding would be easier to understand.
Obviously, glycine binding cannot trigger the conformational change from inward to outward. What
are the possible factors that trigger conformational changes physiologically?
We thank the reviewer for this interesting question. The conformational cycle of GlyT2, like other
SLC6 family members, follows the alternate access mechanism and is driven primarily by the
coupled transport of sodium and chloride ions with the substrate glycine. In this model, only one side
of the binding site is accessible at a time, preventing ion and substrate leakage.
In the outward-facing conformation, sodium ions (and chloride ions, as required by eukaryotic SLC6
family members) bind to their respective sites within the transporter from the extracellular side. The
binding of these driving ions creates a high-affinity environment for substrate binding, enabling
glycine to subsequently bind. Once sodium, chloride, and glycine are all bound, the transporter
undergoes a conformational change to the occluded state, in which the binding sites are sealed off
from both sides of the membrane.
From this occluded state, the transporter transitions to the inward-facing conformation, exposing the
binding sites to the cytoplasmic side. Here, the co-transported Na+ ions, glycine, and Cl– ion are
released sequentially into the cytoplasm. This release destabilizes the inward-facing state, allowing
the transporter to undergo another conformational change and ultimately return to the outward-facing
state. Re-binding of sodium and chloride ions from the extracellular space stabilizes the outward-
open state and resets the transporter for another round of glycine uptake.
In details:
In NSS transporters, “two ligand-dependent networks” cooperate to close the extracellular pathway
and allow the cytoplasmic pathway to open. 1 – One of these networks centers on the interactions
of the substrate carboxyl group with a tyrosine in TM3 (Y287 in GlyT2) and with Na+ bound at the
Na1 site. Mutation of this tyrosine residue in the bacterial homologue LeuT blocks the ability of the
bound substrate to initiate the open-out to open-in conformational change that allows substrate and
Na+ to dissociate to the cytoplasm. 2– The other network involves formation of the salt bridge at
extracellular gate of the pathway between TM1 and TM10 (R216–D633 in GlyT2). Formation of this
network is facilitated by Cl− binding and depends on a conserved glutamine residue in the Cl− binding
site (Q473 in GlyT2). The interaction between Cl− and Q473 in GlyT2, disengages R216 so that it
can interact with D633 to close the extracellular pathway (ref.1,2). Glycine transporters, including
GlyT2, are characterised by tight stoichiometric coupling of Na+, substrate, and Cl− transport (ref.
18
3). Therefore, we would expect that only when Na+, Cl−, and substrate are bound would their
combined conformational effects close the extracellular pathway and allow the cytoplasmic pathway
of GlyT2 to fully open. The effect of Cl− binding, together with the influence of substrate binding on
conformation, further stabilizes the closed extracellular pathway and facilitates opening of the
cytoplasmic pathway to release substrate and ions to the cytoplasm.
The conserved leucine residue on TM1 (L211 in GlyT2, L25 in LeuT) has been shown to play a key
role in the inward-to-outward transition. In the absence of ions (Na+ and Cl–) and substrate, this
leucine occupies the binding pocket, acting as a gatekeeper that prevents ion leak during the return
to the outward-facing state (ref. 4). When the leucine side chain relocates out of the binding pocket,
it creates space for ions binding. Binding of Na⁺ at the Na1 and Na2 sites, together with chloride
binding, stabilizes the outward-open conformation and primes the transporter for glycine binding and
forward transport.
Both allosteric inhibitors of GlyT2, ORG25543 and RPI-GLYT2-82, “lock” the transporter in the
outward-open state through two complementary mechanisms: (1) disrupting the extracellular gate
by breaking the salt bridge involving R216 and D633, thereby preventing opening of the cytoplasmic
pathway and transition toward the inward-facing, and (2) constraining the conserved leucine residue
(L211) outside of the substrate pocket, which further locks GlyT2 in the outward-open
conformation (Because this residue serves as a critical gatekeeper for sodium entry and substrate binding,
its immobilization locks GlyT2 in the outward-open state and prevents the conformational cycling
required for transport). Together, these mechanisms explain how small-molecule binding
allosterically arrests GlyT2 in a non-transporting state, thereby inhibiting glycine uptake.
Inspired by this question, we have added a detailed discussion of the mechanism of transport by
GlyT2 (and other NSS) and inhibition by the allosteric inhibitors in the revised manuscript:
In NSS transporters, two ligand-dependent networks coordinate closure of the extracellular
pathway and opening of the cytoplasmic one. The first involves the substrate carboxyl group
interacting with a tyrosine in TM3 (Y287 in GlyT2) and Na⁺ at the Na1 site; mutation of this
tyrosine in the bacterial homologue LeuT prevents the substrate-induced outward-to-inward
transition53. The second network forms a salt bridge between TM1 and TM10 (R216–D633 in
GlyT2), stabilized by Cl⁻ binding through a conserved glutamine residue in the Cl− binding site
(Q473 in GlyT2). The interaction between Cl− and Q473 in GlyT2, releases R216 to engage D633,
sealing the extracellular gate54,55. In GlyT2, transport of Na⁺, Cl⁻, and glycine is tightly coupled,
and only their combined binding drives full closure of the extracellular pathway and opening of
the cytoplasmic side where the ions and substrate are released56. The conserved leucine residue
on TM1 (L211 in GlyT2, L25 in LeuT) plays a key role in the inward-to-outward transition. The
residue L211 acts as a gatekeeper, occupying the substrate pocket in the absence of ions to prevent
leak during the return to the outward-facing state57 and vacating the pocket upon Na⁺ and Cl⁻
binding to prime the transporter for glycine binding and forward transport.
The allosteric inhibitors ORG25543 and RPI-GLYT2-82 lock GlyT2 in the outward-open state
through two complementary mechanisms: (1) disrupting the extracellular gate by breaking the
salt bridge involving R216 and D633, thereby preventing opening of the cytoplasmic pathway
and transition toward the inward-facing state, and (2) constraining the conserved leucine residue
(L211) outside of the substrate pocket, which further locks GlyT2 in the outward-open
conformation (Fig. 4f,g, and 6). Immobilization of the critical gatekeeper residues blocks
conformational cycling and traps GlyT2 in a non-transporting state, thereby inhibiting glycine
transport.

noted the same phenomenon in the GABA-bound GAT3 structure (unpublished; BioRxiv

Reviewer #5 (Remarks to the Author):
In their work, Cantwell Chater and colleagues develop a reversible inhibitor of the neuronal glycine
transporter GlyT2 that provides analgesia in mouse models of neuropathic pain. To elucidate its
mechanism of action, the authors resolved the structure of human GlyT2 for the first time alone and
in complex with glycine and two different inhibitors, including the newly synthetized one.
Electrophysiology and structural insights, aided by MD simulations, showed that the newly
synthetized compound acts as a reversible allosteric inhibitor that traps the transporter in an outward
facing conformation. Because of its relatively low affinity, the inhibitor shows no on-target side
effects, making it a very promising therapeutical target to treat chronic neuropathic pain.
I believe this study to be highly relevant for the field of neurotransmitter transporters. First, by
capturing GlyT2 at different conformations, including the one bound to its endogenous ligand, the
23
authors set the ground for further mechanistic understanding of its transport cycle. More importantly,
the rational design of a new promising inhibitor of GlyT2 may lay the foundation for further
development of non-opioid pain therapeutics.
The conclusions of the study are sound and supported by a vast array of different methods, including
structural and computational techniques, electrophysiology and animal models.
The manuscript is clear and well written; I found it quite easy to follow through the results although
most techniques used are outside my field of expertise.

simulations (Supplementary Fig. 11d-i). I would even suggest changing the title of the second section
of the results to “hGlyT2 adopts a LeuT fold stabilized by lipids”.

molecules play a structural part, rather than a functional role.

simulations and are free to diffuse within the membrane, including into and out of their binding sites.

environment. As recommended, we have expanded the main text to discuss role of cholesterol

- In Supplementary Fig. 15, RMSD values show that the backbone of the protein takes some time to
equilibrate. RMSD of heavy atoms of the inhibitors also show fluctuations throughout the simulations.
However, the authors perform MM-PBSA only on the first 50 ns of the trajectories, where the protein
has clearly not fully equilibrated. To me, it is not surprising that the MM-PBSA results agree with the
structural data if the initial structure did not have the time to relax. I strongly recommend to perform

24
results, more analysis might be needed, as this could suggest the existence of several different

We thank the reviwer for this remark and would like to point out that the purpose of the MM-PBSA
calculations was to “calculate the enthalpic contribution of each protein residue within the cryo-EM
binding site” to the protein/ligand interactions, to determine which interactions stabilised or
destabilised ligand binding. For this reason, the MM-PBSA was calculated on the first 50 ns of
simulation, during which each ligand was fully contained within its cryo-EM density envelope, when
there were minimal transient changes in the binding mode of RPI-GLYT2-82 and ORG25543
(Supporting Figure 19). These transient changes in ligand RMSD are also noted by the Reviewer.
To further clarify, we would like to point out that the protein backbone structures, in fact, did have
sufficient time to relax in the MD equilibration protocol described in the Methods section. Protein
backbone RMSD plateaued after the first 20 ns of simulation, then fluctuated around the mean of
2.83+/0.44 Å with ORG25543 bound and 2.23 +/- 0.39 Å with RPI-GLYT2-82 bound, for the
remaining 480 ns of simulation. This is well within thermal noise of the protein at 300 K
(doi:10.1002/prot.340220308).
While MM-PBSA remains a powerful “but theoretical tool”, our cryo-EM maps unambiguously depict
the ligands pose, making that the most reliable anchor for our mechanistic interpretation. Therefore,
while we respect the suggestion, we strongly consider our cryo-EM data to provide a definitive
experimental foundation for how these inhibitors bind, which appropriately underpins the
computational analysis.

In the docking with glycine, looking at the Cysteine density. Chater et al. says that “However,
although we observed clear densities for C311 and C320 in glycine-bound hGlyT2d185, we did not
detect a distinct density for the disulfide bridge, suggesting that the cysteine residues may be
reduced in the substrate-bound state”. Does this mean that the C311 and C320 are involved in

We thank the reviewer for this interesting question. It is generally not well established how
specifically this disulfide bridge can affect the conformational state of GlyT2 or any other NSS
member, apart from the general stabilization of the extracellular side of the transporter and especially
the extracellular loop 2. However, the cysteines/disulfide bridge is crucial for protein folding, as seen
for example by mutations in GAT1 (p.Cys164Tyr) (Palmer S. et al. Pediatr Neurol, 2016). We can
only speculate as to what this observation means and given the inherent flexibility of the extracellular
loop 2, we can’t conclude that any differences observed are due to the missing disulfide bridge.
However, it is worth noting that in other substrate-bound SLC6 transporters such as GABA-bound
hGAT1 (PDB 7Y7W, EMDB 33672), glycine-bound hGlyT1 (PDB 8WFI, EMDB 37492), and
dopamine-bound hDAT (PDB 8Y2D, EMDB 38851) we do not observe a continuous cryo-EM density
representative of a formed disulfide bridge at the recommended contour levels, suggesting the
disulfide bridge might be reduced in other substrate-bound SLC6 transporters. The disulfide bridge
may also be reduced in other substrate-bound SLC6 transporters. This is also an effort to encourage
the community to pay closer attention to the density during model building.

inhibitors such as ORG25543 and RPI-GLYT2-82 inhibit glycine transport by preventing

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
I am satisfied with most of the responses by the authors with one exception.
The conditioned place preference (CPP) paradigm should be performed. As outlined in my previous
comment, it will provide important additional data, as it allows assessing the aversive component of
pain. There are actually compounds (adenosine) that reduced withdrawal responses but have no
effects in the CPP, potentially indicating that they lack analgesic efficacy despite being active in
withdrawal response assays.
The authors argue that the test «works best» with reenforcing drugs such as morphine. This is not
correct. On the contrary, reinforcing properties are an important confounding factor. The authors cite
Sufka, Pain 1994 who writes “… the negatively reinforcing properties of analgesic drugs can be
assessed via the CPP paradigm. In addition, this paradigm offers greater clinical relevance as
animals determine drug efficacy without the involvement of high-intensity, phasic nociceptive
stimulation.” Already the first publication (on the use of CPP in analgesia research (King et al., Nat
Neurosci, 2009; PMID 19783992) showed that CPP works well with drugs without reenforcing
properties (clonidine, conotoxin, lidocaine). Another more recent example is Neumann et al., PAIN
2021 (PMID 32773599), who have successsfully studied a drug enhancing inhibitory
neurotransmission in the spinal cord.
We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful comment. We agree that CPP can provide supportive
evidence when a positive signal is observed; however, it is equally important to emphasize that
absence of an analgesic effect in CPP does not equate to a lack of analgesia. Across multiple drug
classes, clinically effective analgesics often produce inconsistent CPP outcomes. For example,
NSAIDs, despite being robust and clinically reliable analgesics, often fail to produce CPP, even when
their antinociceptive effects are clearly demonstrated in standard behavioural assays. Thus, CPP
can be informative when an analgesic effect is observed, but a lack of effect cannot be taken as
conclusive evidence that a compound does not relieve pain. This makes CPP unsuitable as a
universal confirmatory assay in early-stage analgesic studies. We consider that performing CPP in
the current manuscript would be unlikely to produce an unambiguous, mechanistically informative
result that changes the interpretation of our anti-allodynia findings. The CPP readout risks adding
interpretational ambiguity (reward vs analgesia) rather than clarity, especially at this early,
mechanistic stage of drug development.
We have also directly addressed the reviewer’s concern that enhanced glycinergic inhibition might
reduce withdrawal responses via motor weakness rather than genuine analgesia. To resolve this,
we incorporated targeted motor-control experiments (grip strength). These data demonstrate that at
analgesic doses there are no motor deficits coincident with the anti-allodynic window, and that mild,
transient impairment only appears at a supramaximal dose with a distinct time course from the
analgesic effect. These findings directly address the confound raised by the reviewer and support
the conclusion that reduced withdrawal responses arise from analgesia rather than motor weakness.
In addition, we would like to emphasise that the concern raised by the reviewer – that reduced
withdrawal responses may not reflect true analgesia, as seen with compounds like adenosine that
reduce withdrawal endpoints but have no effects in the CPP, has now been directly addressed by
the inclusion of “cold allodynia” testing. Cold allodynia is a distinct and clinically relevant modality of
neuropathic pain, and efficacy in this assay provides modality-independent evidence for analgesic
action. RPI-GLYT2-82 produced robust and dose-dependent reversal of cold allodynia in the CCI
model, with significant reductions in acetone-evoked responses at both 50 and 100 mg/kg and peak
efficacy comparable to gabapentin (Fig. 5b). These effects occurred in the absence of motor deficits
at analgesic doses, as demonstrated by rotarod and grip-strength assays, and therefore cannot be
attributed to drug-induced weakness or impaired responsiveness. Together, the demonstration of
efficacy across multiple sensory modalities (mechanical and cold allodynia), combined with specific
motor-control data, provides strong convergent evidence of true analgesic activity, independent of
any motor confound or artefactual suppression of withdrawal behaviours.
The authors have addressed my questions. It is a pity that efforts to determine the binding affinity
between ORG25543, RPI-GLYT2-82 and GlyT2 are failed. But the results in the author rebuttal is
rather convincing. I understand that the micelle environment could interfere the ligand binding in the
purified GlyT2. Other problems about sodium, chloride and cholesterols in GlyT2 transport are all
addressed properly. The proposed inhibitory mechanism of ORG25543 and RPI-GLYT2-82 is
reasonable.
Personally I think the manuscript is a good candidate to publish on Nature Communications.
We thank the reviewer for their contributions.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
I am satisfied with most of the responses by the authors with one exception.
The conditioned place preference (CPP) paradigm should be performed. As outlined in my previous comment, it will provide important additional data, as it allows assessing the aversive component of pain. There are actually compounds (adenosine) that reduced withdrawal responses but have no effects in the CPP, potentially indicating that they lack analgesic efficacy despite being active in withdrawal response assays.
The authors argue that the test «works best» with reenforcing drugs such as morphine. This is not correct. On the contrary, reinforcing properties are an important confounding factor. The authors cite Sufka, Pain 1994 who writes “… the negatively reinforcing properties of analgesic drugs can be assessed via the CPP paradigm. In addition, this paradigm offers greater clinical relevance as animals determine drug efficacy without the involvement of high-intensity, phasic nociceptive stimulation.” Already the first publication (on the use of CPP in analgesia research (King et al., Nat Neurosci, 2009; PMID 19783992) showed that CPP works well with drugs without reenforcing properties (clonidine, conotoxin, lidocaine). Another more recent example is Neumann et al., PAIN 2021 (PMID 32773599), who have successsfully studied a drug enhancing inhibitory neurotransmission in the spinal cord.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The authors have addressed my questions. It is a pity that efforts to determine the binding affinity between ORG25543, RPI-GLYT2-82 and GlyT2 are failed. But the results in the author rebuttal is rather convincing. I understand that the micelle environment could interfere the ligand binding in the purified GlyT2. Other problems about sodium, chloride and cholesterols in GlyT2 transport are all addressed properly. The proposed inhibitory mechanism of ORG25543 and RPI-GLYT2-82 is reasonable.
Personally I think the manuscript is a good candidate to publish on Nature Communications.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_5:
I thank the authors for addressing all my points. I just have two comments:
1. Regarding the MM-PBSA, they wrote: "We thank the reviewer for this remark and would like to point out that the purpose of the MM-PBSA calculations was to “calculate the enthalpic contribution of each protein residue within the cryo-EM binding site” to the protein/ligand interactions, to determine which interactions stabilised or destabilised ligand binding." I thank the authors for the clarification. If the purpose of the MM-PBSA is solely to calculate the enthalpic contribution within the cryo-EM structure, then it is indeed fine to just use the first 50 ns of the simulation. In my opinion, however, this point is not clearly made in the text. I did not find the quote the authors refer to anywhere in the current version, perhaps it got lost during the revision process. In any case, I strongly recommend the authors to add the quoted sentence in the results section of the main text.
A further source of misunderstanding is that, in Supplementary Figure 19, the MM-PBSA energy decomposition plots are displayed in the same panel as the density heat maps; in the captions, the authors write that the density heat maps were obtained from the total simulation time of 1500 ns, so one gets the impression the MM-PBSA energy decomposition has been calculated for the same time range. The authors only specify that they used only 50 ns of the simulation for the plot of the relative binding enthalpy of ORG25543 and RPI-GLYT2-82, but I would strongly suggest to specify in the figure caption that this is the case for all three MM-PBSA plots displayed.
2. I noticed that the authors have added new docking results. These are in my opinion consistent with the rest of the results and further strengthen the model of allosteric inhibition. I would just make a small clarification in the nomenclature: I don’t like the term “docking simulation”, because it can be misleading. Technically speaking, the authors first did a docking calculation of the binding pose, and then used MD simulations to assess the stability of this binding pose. I recommend rephrasing the sentence “to assess whether glycine can bind to inhibitor-bound hGlyT2 conformations obtained by cryo-EM, we performed 50 ns docking simulations“ to something like “to assess whether glycine can bind to inhibitor-bound hGlyT2 conformations obtained by cryo-EM, we first docked this molecule onto the inhibitor-bound structure and assessed the stability of the binding poses using MD simulations.”
After the authors have addressed these two points, I’m happy to suggest acceptance of this article.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_6:
Upon re-examining the revised manuscript, I acknowledge that the authors have improved the quality of the functional data increasing the value of the data reported with new information that was previously missing. Nevertheless, several substantial issues remain to be addressed.
Firstly, after reviewing the authors’ responses to my earlier comments, I still do not find an answer. My (and of another reviewer) original request concerned experiments involving the MATs transporter, whereas the response provided refers instead to GlyT1(see the end of pag 26 beginning of 27 of the responses to the reviewers). Consequently, I must reiterate my initial question: "First, the data collected about GlyT2 in Figure 1 must also be collected for GLYT1. The absence of effect, SERT, DAT and NET must be shown. These last two (DAT and NET) are to be tested because usually any compound interacting with SERT has an action also on the other monoamine transporters (even if the data about the binding seems to exclude this possibility). My request was to have these data obtained in the same model (Xenopus laevis oocytes) expressing MATs in the presence of the compound. This would be a easy and informative experiment, allowing the authors to assess whether the compound exerts similar or distinct effects within the same experimental system.
For the remaining points raised by this reviewer, the responses and the data provided are satisfactory. I would, however, like to point out one typo error: the equation referenced is the Michaelis–Menten equation, not “Monten.”
In conclusion, the manuscript has gratly improved, but addressing the experimental point above is necessary to fully substantiate the authors’ claims.

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
I am satisfied with most of the responses by the authors with one exception.
The conditioned place preference (CPP) paradigm should be performed. As outlined in my previous comment, it will provide important additional data, as it allows assessing the aversive component of pain. There are actually compounds (adenosine) that reduced withdrawal responses but have no effects in the CPP, potentially indicating that they lack analgesic efficacy despite being active in withdrawal response assays.
The authors argue that the test «works best» with reenforcing drugs such as morphine. This is not correct. On the contrary, reinforcing properties are an important confounding factor. The authors cite Sufka, Pain 1994 who writes “… the negatively reinforcing properties of analgesic drugs can be assessed via the CPP paradigm. In addition, this paradigm offers greater clinical relevance as animals determine drug efficacy without the involvement of high-intensity, phasic nociceptive stimulation.” Already the first publication (on the use of CPP in analgesia research (King et al., Nat Neurosci, 2009; PMID 19783992) showed that CPP works well with drugs without reenforcing properties (clonidine, conotoxin, lidocaine). Another more recent example is Neumann et al., PAIN 2021 (PMID 32773599), who have successsfully studied a drug enhancing inhibitory neurotransmission in the spinal cord.
We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful comment. We agree that CPP can provide supportive evidence when a positive signal is observed; however, it is equally important to emphasize that absence of an analgesic effect in CPP does not equate to a lack of analgesia. Across multiple drug classes, clinically effective analgesics often produce inconsistent CPP outcomes. For example, NSAIDs, despite being robust and clinically reliable analgesics, often fail to produce CPP, even when their antinociceptive effects are clearly demonstrated in standard behavioural assays. Thus, CPP can be informative when an analgesic effect is observed, but a lack of effect cannot be taken as conclusive evidence that a compound does not relieve pain. This makes CPP unsuitable as a universal confirmatory assay in early-stage analgesic studies. We consider that performing CPP in the current manuscript would be unlikely to produce an unambiguous, mechanistically informative result that changes the interpretation of our anti-allodynia findings. The CPP readout risks adding interpretational ambiguity (reward vs analgesia) rather than clarity, especially at this early, mechanistic stage of drug development.
We have also directly addressed the reviewer’s concern that enhanced glycinergic inhibition might reduce withdrawal responses via motor weakness rather than genuine analgesia. To resolve this, we incorporated targeted motor-control experiments (grip strength). These data demonstrate that at analgesic doses there are no motor deficits coincident with the anti-allodynic window, and that mild, transient impairment only appears at a supramaximal dose with a distinct time course from the analgesic effect. These findings directly address the confound raised by the reviewer and support the conclusion that reduced withdrawal responses arise from analgesia rather than motor weakness.
In addition, we would like to emphasise that the concern raised by the reviewer – that reduced withdrawal responses may not reflect true analgesia, as seen with compounds like adenosine that reduce withdrawal endpoints but have no effects in the CPP, has now been directly addressed by the inclusion of “cold allodynia” testing. Cold allodynia is a distinct and clinically relevant modality of neuropathic pain, and efficacy in this assay provides modality-independent evidence for analgesic action. RPI-GLYT2-82 produced robust and dose-dependent reversal of cold allodynia in the CCI model, with significant reductions in acetone-evoked responses at both 50 and 100 mg/kg and peak efficacy comparable to gabapentin (Fig. 5b). These effects occurred in the absence of motor deficits at analgesic doses, as demonstrated by rotarod and grip-strength assays, and therefore cannot be attributed to drug-induced weakness or impaired responsiveness. Together, the demonstration of efficacy across multiple sensory modalities (mechanical and cold allodynia), combined with specific motor-control data, provides strong convergent evidence of true analgesic activity, independent of any motor confound or artefactual suppression of withdrawal behaviours.
The authors have addressed my questions. It is a pity that efforts to determine the binding affinity between ORG25543, RPI-GLYT2-82 and GlyT2 are failed. But the results in the author rebuttal is rather convincing. I understand that the micelle environment could interfere the ligand binding in the purified GlyT2. Other problems about sodium, chloride and cholesterols in GlyT2 transport are all addressed properly. The proposed inhibitory mechanism of ORG25543 and RPI-GLYT2-82 is reasonable.
Personally I think the manuscript is a good candidate to publish on Nature Communications.
We thank the reviewer for their contributions.

Regarding the comment: “First, the data collected about GlyT2 in Figure 1 must also be collected for GLYT1”, as shown in Fig. 1h, RPI-GLYT2-82 produces only ~6% inhibition at 10 μM on GlyT1. This absence of measurable activity is why the additional experiments (IC₅₀ curves, Na⁺-dependence, washout behaviour) cannot be performed for GlyT1, as these assays require a compound that actually inhibits the transporter.
We agree with the reviewer that “compounds interacting with SERT usually also have an action on the other monoamine transporters.” For this reason, we conducted a full MAT selectivity profile for RPI-GLYT2-82 early in the study. We also appreciate the comments from Reviewer #6 for proposing that we repeat our experiments conducted in Figure 1 with monoamine transporters (MATs): SERT, DAT and NET. Whilst this is an admirable goal, it is unlikely to provide reliable data that would enhance the current study beyond what we have already provided as the effect of RPI-GLYT2-82 on the relevant monoamine transporters could not “technically” be studied in X. laevis oocytes used for assessing the effect on GlyT1 and GlyT2. We would like to elaborate on this:
Our in vitro characterization of RPI-GLYT2-82 was conducted in Xenopus laevis oocytes which is a robust expression system for the glycine transporters (hGlyT1 and hGlyT2). However, “hNET does not express in this expression system” and therefore neither two-electrode voltage clamp electrophysiology nor radiolabeled uptake is possible in oocytes. Please see the following reference: (https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/3-540-29784-7_2). As expected, we could not find any studies that has successfully expressed hNET in oocytes or reported any current measurements.
The vast majority of studies on hSERT and hDAT utilise 3H-substrate uptake assays using mammalian cells expressing the recombinant transporters, or inhibition of 3H-antagonists binding, which are the gold standard methodologies that allow comparison with other studies. Oocytes have been used in ”only ~7 papers1-7 in the last 30 years” (out of many 1000’s of papers) and in most cases application of serotonin to oocytes expressing hSERT generate only ~20 nA currents. This is at about the limit for reliable measurements and in our experience (as we also tried hSERT in oocytes) it has not provided a reliable signal to noise level to provide an accurate assessment of the activity of inhibitors. Experiments with hDAT are even less reliable than hSERT and often involve the ”murine version of DAT” to provide sufficient currents which are more robust compared to human DAT4,6.
In contrast, oocytes are an excellent system for measuring glycine transport currents because they generate currents in the range of 50-300 nA.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Chronic neuropathic pain, caused by nerve damage or disease, is increasing in prevalence, but current treatments are ineffective and over-reliant on opioids. The neuronal glycine transporter, GlyT2, regulates inhibitory glycinergic neurotransmission and represents a promising target for new analgesics. However, most GlyT2 inhibitors cause significant side effects, in part due to irreversible inhibition at analgesic doses. Here we develop a reversible inhibitor of GlyT2, RPI-GLYT2-82, and identify its binding site by determining cryo-EM structures of human GlyT2. We capture three fundamental conformational states of GlyT2 in the substrate-free state, and bound to either glycine, RPI-GLYT2-82 or the pseudo-irreversible inhibitor ORG25543. We demonstrate that RPI-GLYT2-82 dissociates from GlyT2 faster than ORG25543, providing analgesia in mouse neuropathic pain models without on-target side-effects or addiction liability. Our data provide a mechanistic understanding of allosteric inhibition of glycine transport, enabling structure-based design of non-opioid analgesics.

---

## Introduction

Chronic neuropathic pain affects 7–10% of the population yet only one in four of these patients respond to the gold standard treatment, pregabalin. Furthermore, because the efficacy of pregabalin is limited and accompanied by dose-dependent side effects, there is an over-reliance on opioid medications, exacerbating opioid use disorder and its associated mortality1,2. The rising incidence of neuropathic pain has therefore created an urgent need for the development of safe and effective analgesics that circumvent the opioid mechanism by targeting new pathways2.

A key feature of neuropathic pain is a reduction of glycinergic neurotransmission in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord – an adaptation that impairs our capacity to distinguish between painful and harmless stimuli3. Glycine is an inhibitory neurotransmitter that hyperpolarises postsynaptic neurons by binding to and opening Cl–-permeable glycine receptors. In the central nervous system, the concentration of extracellular glycine is tightly regulated by glycine transporters 1 and 2 (GlyT1 and GlyT2). GlyT1 is expressed at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses, whereas GlyT2 is exclusively localized to the presynaptic neurons of inhibitory synapses, primarily in the spinal cord4. GlyT2 thus plays a key role in regulating glycinergic neurotransmission by controlling glycine receptor activity on postsynaptic neurons and by recycling glycine for subsequent release from presynaptic neurons5–8.

GlyT2 (encoded by SLC6A5) belongs to the solute carrier 6 (SLC6) subfamily of secondary active neurotransmitter/sodium symporters (NSSs)9,10. NSSs are membrane proteins that operate via an alternating access mechanism, whereby transmembrane helices undergo conformational rearrangements during the transport cycle that alternately expose the substrate-binding site to each side of the membrane. In eukaryotic NSSs, binding of extracellular substrate and initiation of the transport cycle is dependent on a Na+ and Cl− gradient, such that GlyT2 co-transports three Na+ ions and one Cl− ion with each glycine11–13. Upon ion and substrate binding, access to the extracellular environment is occluded as the transporter transitions from an outward-facing to an inward-facing conformation, followed by release of solutes.

Several competitive and non-competitive SLC6 inhibitors have been developed that target either outward or inward-facing conformations of these transporters14–25. At glycinergic synapses, competitive GlyT2 inhibitors are likely to be ineffective due to the high concentrations of glycine in the cleft during synaptic transmission, whereas non-competitive inhibitors that target allosteric sites will be more effective8. Allosteric inhibitors are also more likely to result in subtype selectivity as substrate binding sites show little amino acid divergence across the NSS superfamily. Furthermore, because glycine is the only known substrate transported by GlyT2, the chemical space that can be explored for orthosteric inhibition is restricted26. Interestingly, ORG25543 (4-(benzyloxy)-N-{[1-(dimethylamino)cyclopentyl]methyl}−3,5-dimethoxybenzamide) is a potent, pseudo-irreversible, and non-competitive27 inhibitor of GlyT2 that provides analgesia in animal models of neuropathic pain28–31, without affecting acute or inflammatory pain thresholds28. In rat spinal cord slices, ORG25543 enhances tonic glycinergic neurotransmission and prolongs the decay time course of both miniature and evoked glycinergic inhibitory postsynaptic currents, suggesting that its effects are likely due to elevated extracellular glycine concentrations32. However, the compound did not progress to clinical use due to its narrow therapeutic index and significant on-target side effects, including tremors, seizures, and mortality at the maximal analgesic dose. These effects, which resemble the phenotype of the mouse GlyT2-/- knockout, are likely due to the high affinity and slow dissociation rate of ORG2554328,29. Indeed, siRNA knockdown of GlyT2 to 30% of wild-type (WT) levels results in prolonged analgesia without confounding side effects in mouse models of neuropathic pain33. In addition, the endogenous bioactive lipid N-arachidonoyl glycine and synthetic derivatives such as oleoyl-D-lysine cause partial inhibition of GlyT2 comparable to knockdown studies and provide analgesia without side effects. However, the poor pharmacokinetics of these bioactive lipids prevented progression to clinical trials28,34,35. Recently, an ORG25543-based benzamide, opiranserin (VVZ-149), reached a confirmatory phase 3 trial for the treatment of post-colectomy pain36,37, validating the importance of GlyT2 as a target for new pain therapeutics. Opiranserin, however, only shows moderately potent inhibitory activity on GlyT238.

Here we synthesize a potency-tuned analogue of ORG25543, RPI-GLYT2-82 (1-benzoyl-N-((4-(dimethylamino)tetrahydro-2H-pyran-4-yl)methyl)indoline-5-carboxamide) and determine its suitability for development as a treatment for neuropathic pain. We determine the structures of human GlyT2 (hGlyT2) – without substrate (inward-open conformation) and bound to either glycine (inward-occluded state), ORG25543 (outward-open state), or RPI-GLYT2-82 (outward-open state) – and confirm the allosteric action of both inhibitors. We further show that RPI-GLYT2-82 is efficacious at alleviating allodynia in both chronic constriction injury (CCI) and partial sciatic nerve ligation (PSNL) mouse models, without any side effects at the maximal analgesic dose. Our study thus reveals the molecular mechanism of allosteric inhibition of glycine transport, providing a framework by which new analgesics can be developed.

---

## Results

RPI-GLYT2-82 is a non-competitive GlyT2 inhibitor
The narrow therapeutic index of ORG25543 has been attributed to its slow dissociation rate, suggesting that ORG25543-based compounds with improved reversibility may decrease on-target side effects and toxicity29,39,40. To overcome the liabilities associated with ORG25543 while simultaneously introducing chemical novelty into the GlyT2 inhibitor scaffold, we pursued the design of rigidified benzamide derivatives with reduced conformational flexibility, a strategy anticipated to enhance passive permeability and improve overall drug-like properties. Among the structural variants examined, ring-constrained heterocycles, most notably indolines, emerged as effective and structurally innovative isosteric replacements for the tri-alkoxybenzamide motif of ORG25543, maintaining both GlyT2 inhibitory potency and reversible binding kinetics. A subsequent integrated drug discovery effort focused on these conformationally restricted indoline scaffolds ultimately yielded the allosteric GlyT2 inhibitor RPI-GLYT2-82 (Fig. 1a, b, and Supplementary methods).

We first characterized the inhibitory action of RPI-GLYT2-82 by expressing WT hGlyT2 (hGlyT2WT) in Xenopus oocytes and using the two-electrode voltage clamp technique to record glycine-induced transport currents in the presence of different concentrations of the compound. RPI-GLYT2-82 behaved as a non-competitive inhibitor (Fig. 1c, and Supplementary Table 1) with a half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) of 554 nM (Fig. 1d). This confirmed the lower inhibition potency of RPI-GLYT2-82 for hGlyT2WT than ORG25543, which displayed an IC50 of 11.4 nM (Fig. 1e). Glycine-induced transport currents recovered to pre-inhibition levels within five minutes of RPI-GLYT2-82 removal, indicating a markedly faster transport recovery rate than ORG25543, which required 30 minutes for currents to be restored to only 12.5% of pre-inhibitor levels (Fig. 1f, g, and Supplementary Fig. 1). Together, these data show that RPI-GLYT-82 is a non-competitive GlyT2 inhibitor with reduced potency compared to ORG25543. Like ORG25543, RPI-GLYT2-82 is selective for GlyT2 over GlyT1 (Fig. 1h). Interestingly, while the inhibition of transport by both compounds appears to be Na⁺-independent, RPI-GLYT2-82 exhibits slightly increased potency under lower Na⁺ concentrations, whereas inhibition by ORG25543 remains unaffected (Fig. 1i, j).

hGlyT2 adopts a LeuT fold
To understand the mechanism by which ORG25543 and RPI-GLYT-82 inhibit GlyT2, we sought to determine the structures of hGlyT2 in the absence and presence of these inhibitors and the substrate glycine. Because the N-terminus of hGlyT2 is predicted to be largely unstructured and its deletion does not affect trafficking to the plasma membrane or glycine transport41, we created a construct lacking residues 2-185 (hGlyT2Δ185) to facilitate expression and purification. hGlyT2Δ185 exhibited a similar half-maximal effective concentration (EC50) for glycine transport, and similar IC50 values for both ORG25543 and RPI-GLYT2-82, to full-length hGlyT2WT (Fig. 1d, e, k).

We purified hGlyT2Δ185 in mixed micelles containing lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol (LMNG), glyco-diosgenin (GDN), and cholesteryl hemisuccinate (CHS) at a ratio of 1.0:1.0:0.1 to generate monodisperse and homogenous hGlyT2Δ185 (Supplementary Fig. 2) for cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) studies. This enabled structures of hGlyT2Δ185 in the absence of substrate and bound to glycine, ORG25543, or RPI-GLYT2-82 to be determined at 2.97 Å, 3.02 Å, 2.49 Å, and 2.79 Å resolution, respectively (Fig. 2a–h, Supplementary Fig. 3–6, and Supplementary Table 2). The high-quality of the resulting density maps enabled unambiguous modelling of all 12 transmembrane (TM) helices, revealing unwinding of TMs 1 and 6 approximately halfway across the membrane – a characteristic feature of the substrate binding site in SLC6 transporters (Fig. 2, and Supplementary Fig. 7–10). We were also able to model the intracellular and extracellular loops, except parts of extracellular loop 2 (EL2; residues 302–393) due to its high degree of flexibility (Fig. 2, and Supplementary Fig. 7-10), as well as the position of bound ligands and ions. The conserved disulfide bridge between C311 and C320 in EL2 is present in the inhibitor-bound and substrate-free structures (Supplementary Fig. 7, 9–11). However, although we observed clear densities for C311 and C320 in glycine-bound hGlyT2Δ185, we did not detect a distinct density for the disulfide bridge, suggesting that the cysteine residues may be reduced in the substrate-bound state (Supplementary Fig. 8). The overall architecture adopted by hGlyT2 is characteristic of SLC6 transporters: an inverted pseudo-twofold symmetric organisation of TMs 1–5 relative to TMs 6–10 (Fig. 2, and Supplementary Fig. 7-10), known as the LeuT fold due to its identification in the bacterial amino acid importer LeuT42.

GlyT2 and related SLC6 transporters are modulated by cholesterol31,43–46. Accordingly, we observed several cholesterol-like features in our hGlyT2Δ185 density maps, which were of sufficient resolution to be modelled in our substrate-free and inhibitor-bound structures (Supplementary Fig. 12). In these three structures, we observed a density consistent with a cholesterol (CHOL) molecule in an inner leaflet pocket formed by TM2, TM7, and TM11, equivalent to the previously reported CHOL2 site17,20,21. We identified an additional neighbouring density where we modelled a CHS molecule (CHOL5). These two molecules form hydrogen bonds with N674 (IL5). Interestingly, while the cholesterol at the CHOL2 site appears to be conserved, this asparagine residue is not conserved among NSS family members. In the Drosophila dopamine transporter (dDAT) and human serotonin transporter (hSERT) it is a glycine residue, in human DAT (hDAT) a serine, and in hGlyT1 and LeuT a proline (Supplementary Figs. 11, 12). We modelled a second CHS molecule adjacent to, but distinct from, the CHOL1 site (CHOL6)19,21. This CHOL6 site lies parallel to and interacts with TM7. Above CHOL6, we modelled a cholesterol molecule in another site, CHOL7, formed by TM5, TM7, and EL4 (Supplementary Fig. 12). Two lipid densities were observed in CHOL6 and CHOL7 sites in a recent hDAT structure20. We further modelled a cholesterol molecule into a site that partially overlaps with CHOL3, and CHOL5 site proposed in molecular dynamics simulations of dDAT (named CHOL3’ in GlyT2)17,18,47. This cholesterol is embedded within the protein, at a methionine-rich site formed by TMs 3, 9, 10 and 12 (Supplementary Fig. 12), in contrast to its alignment with the membrane in other SLC6 structures.

We further examined the stability of sterols in the inhibitor-bound GlyT2 structures and found that most remained stably bound throughout the simulations (Supplementary Fig. 12d–l). However, the cholesterol molecule at the CHOL3’ site in the RPI-GLYT2-82-bound structure sampled multiple conformations while maintaining contact with the site, suggesting local flexibility in this region. Because this feature, along with other sterol molecules we modelled, is consistently present in all hGlyT2Δ185 structures in three different conformational states, we suggest that these sterols act primarily as important structural stabilisers of hGlyT2 rather than as regulatory elements. We did not observe any clear cholesterol-like densities at CHOL1 or CHOL4 sites17.

Substrate-free hGlyT2 is in an inward-open state
Despite inclusion of the GlyT2 inhibitor oleoyl-D-lysine throughout purification, we did not observe any density corresponding to the inhibitor. The low solubility of the compound likely prevented it from remaining in sufficient concentration in solution to bind effectively. We therefore present this structure as the substrate-free state of hGlyT2Δ185 (Fig. 2, and Supplementary Fig. 3, 7).

We captured substrate-free hGlyT2Δ185 in an inward-open conformation in which the extracellular gate is closed due to formation of a conserved salt bridge between residues R216 (TM1b) and D633 (TM10) (Cα-Cα distance of 9.8 Å). Solvation of TM5 and protrusion of TM1 into the micelle creates a large open cavity facing the intracellular milieu. The intracellular part of TM5 is unwound, just before the helix-breaking G419(X9)P429 (Gly(X9)Pro) motif, allowing water from the intracellular space to access the second Na+-binding site (Na2)48. The N-terminal segment of TM1 (TM1a) is bent away from the core of the protein, opening the pathway for solute to be released into the intracellular side. This splaying of TM1 disrupts the interaction between TM1a and the hydrophobic patch on the intracellular part of hGlyT2Δ185 that is present in other outward-facing or inward-occluded NSS structures17,49,50 as well as our outward-facing conformations of hGlyT2Δ185 (Fig. 2e, and Supplementary Fig. 13).

We observed a clear density for Cl− in the substrate-free cryo-EM map of hGlyT2Δ185. This Cl– is coordinated by conserved residues Y233 (TM2), Q473 (TM6a), S477 (unwound region of TM6a), N509 (TM7), and S513 (TM7) at a mean coordination distance of 3.1 Å ± 0.4 (Fig. 3). We did not, however, observe any densities for Na+ at Na1, Na2, or the putative Na3 site, consistent with an inward-open conformational state of the transporter16,50 (Fig. 3).

Glycine-bound hGlyT2 is in an inward-occluded state
Glycine binds within a cavity at the centre of hGlyT2 formed by residues from TMs 1, 3, 6, and 8 (Figs. 2 and 4a, b). The glycine-binding pocket is midway through the membrane bilayer and inaccessible from both extracellular and intracellular sides, indicative of an occluded state of the transporter. The extracellular gate residues, R216 and D633, form a salt bridge (Cα-Cα distance of 9.6 Å), which precludes access from the extracellular milieu. The guanidinium of R216 forms a cation-π interaction with the phenyl group of conserved F476 (TM6a), which sterically blocks the extracellular pathway. The Cα of F476 is 11.3 Å from the Cα of conserved Y287 (TM3), which together cap the glycine binding site (Fig. 4b). The intracellular permeation pathway is occluded by TM1a, which has a more perpendicular arrangement to the membrane than in the substrate-free state (Fig. 2b, f, and Supplementary Fig. 13). The distorted density observed in the intracellular half of TM5 (residues 415–419) (Supplementary Fig. 8) suggests an unwound region preceding the conserved helix-breaking Gly(X9)Pro motif, creating a solvent pathway from the intracellular milieu to Na247, indicative of an inward-occluded state of glycine-bound hGlyT2.

The carboxylate group of glycine forms hydrogen bonds with the backbone nitrogen atoms of G210 and G212 (TM1), the hydroxyl group of T578 (TM8), and more distantly, a weak hydrogen bond with the hydroxyl group of Y287 (TM3). Although the binding mode of glycine’s carboxylate group resembles that of other α-amino acid transporters, including closely related GlyT1, the positioning of the amino group differs25. In hGlyT2, the amino group of glycine appears to form a hydrogen bond with the side-chain hydroxyl of S479 (unwound region of TM6) and is further coordinated by the backbone carbonyl oxygens of Y207 and A208 on TM1, whereas in GlyT1, it adopts a different orientation to interact with the backbone of TM6 residues (Fig. 4c). Residue 479 is a glycine in GlyT1, and the corresponding mutation in GlyT2 (S479G) markedly increases the EC50 for glycine transport, confirming the importance of this residue for substrate transport by hGlyT226,31. The binding pocket for glycine is further constrained by W482 in the conserved (G/A/C)ΦG motif (A481W482G483 in hGlyT2) on the non-helical region of TM6, which allows different sized ligands to be accommodated by the various SLC6 family members51. A conserved glutamate residue in TM2, E248, coordinates the AWG loop via a direct hydrogen bond with backbone nitrogen of A481 – an interaction that is conserved among SLC6 transporters51.

A density for Cl− is clearly apparent in the cryo-EM map of glycine-bound hGlyT2Δ185, coordinated by the same residues as the substrate-free state (Y233, Q473, S477, N509 and S513) at a mean coordination distance of 3.2 Å ± 0.5 (Fig. 3, and Supplementary Fig. 14). We also observed a prominent (13.5 r.m.s.d.) signal for Na+ at Na2, with distorted octahedral coordination by the side chain of D577 (TM8), the backbone carbonyl oxygens of G206 (TM1), Y207 (TM1), V209 (TM1), L574 (TM8), T578 (TM8), and a cytoplasmic water molecule (mean coordination distance of 2.9 Å ± 0.4), similar to previous inward-occluded NSS structures48 (Fig. 3c). We did not observe any densities for Na+ at Na1 or the putative Na3 site. The conserved S477 residue, equivalent to the Na+-coordinating S317 residue at Na1 in GlyT1, is rotated away from the substrate-binding site in glycine-bound hGlyT2, which may suggest that this inward-occluded conformation is in a transitional state.

ORG25543 and RPI-GLYT2-82 lock hGlyT2 in an outward-open state
In the presence of either ORG25543 or RPI-GLYT2-82, the central substrate-binding site of hGlyT2Δ185 is accessible to solvent via the extracellular vestibule, indicating that the inhibitors lock the transporter in an outward-open conformation. The Cα-Cα distance between the two extracellular gating residues, R216 and D633, is 13.9 Å in both ORG25543- and RPI-GLYT2-82-bound structures, consistent with previous outward-facing NSS structures17,18. The cytoplasmic pathway is closed by the location of TM1a within the protein core, allowing the conserved residue W194 to plug a hydrophobic pocket formed by residues on TMs 1, 5, 6, and 7 on the intracellular face of GlyT2 (Fig. 2, and Supplementary Fig. 11, 13).

In both inhibitor-bound structures, there is a clear density for a Cl−, which is coordinated by four of the same residues as those in both inward-facing confirmations (Y233, Q473, S477, and S513; mean coordination distance of 2.8 Å ± 0.3 and 2.9 Å ± 0.5 for ORG25543- and RPI-GLYT2-82 bound structures, respectively. However, Cl− is not directly coordinated by the fifth residue N509 and instead interacts with this residue via a water molecule (Fig. 3d, e). We did not observe any densities for Na+ at Na2 or the putative Na3 site12,13, consistent with ORG2554327 and likely RPI-GLYT2-82, binding being Na+-independent (Fig. 1i, j). We observed a prominent (9.7 r.m.s.d.) signal for a non-protein density in the Na1 site of both inhibitor-bound structures. We initially assigned this density as a water molecule because one of the main Na+ coordinating residues required for the stable octahedral ion coordination geometry, N213 (TM1b), had rotated away from Na1 to interact with the respective inhibitor (Fig. 3d, e). Modelling of the protein complex with water in the Na1 site using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations showed that extracellular Na+ spontaneously bound to this site in four out of six replicate simulations and the site remained occupied by Na+ throughout 50% of the 3000 ns combined replicate simulations (Supplementary Fig. 15, and Supplementary Table 3). As a result, we subsequently modelled Na+ at the Na1 site, coordinated by the backbone carbonyl oxygens of A208 (TM1) and S477 (TM6) as well as a water molecule, reminiscent of a loosely bound hydrated Na+ exposed to the extracellular space (Fig. 3 and Supplementary Fig. 15).

The increased potency of RPI-GLYT2-82 at lower Na⁺ concentrations likely reflects reduced competition of the compound with Na⁺ for N213 coordination, under partially depleted Na⁺ conditions. In contrast, the potency of ORG25543 remains unchanged, likely due to its inherently high potency that renders it insensitive to local Na⁺ occupancy at the Na1 site (Fig. 1i, j).

ORG25543 and RPI-GLYT2-82 occupy an allosteric site
The cryo-EM densities of ORG25543 and RPI-GLYT2-82 were of high quality allowing unambiguous assignment of the respective poses when bound to hGlyT2Δ185 (Fig. 4d, e). We modelled the inhibitors in an allosteric pocket sandwiched between TM1b, TM10, and EL4 that is lined with predominantly hydrophobic residues from TMs 1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10 and EL4 (Fig. 4f, g). The scaffold of ORG25543 and RPI-GLYT2-82 has four key substituents (R1–R4) (Fig. 4h, i). In ORG25543 and RPI-GLYT2-82, respectively, these substituents are: the central benzamide phenyl ring and the central indoline (R1), benzyloxy, and benzoyl phenyl rings (R2), cyclopentyl and tetrahydropyran rings (R3), and the pendant ammonium in both compounds (R4). For both inhibitors, the central R1 group is stacked between W215 (TM1b) and P543 (EL4), and the distal R2 ring is caged by a network of residues including W215 (TM1b), I520 (TM7), Y550 (EL4), and F567 (TM8) as well as A546 (EL4) and M570 (TM8). The R3 rings are located in a relatively large, solvent-exposed pocket, and stabilized by the hydrophobic residues I290 (TM3), P543 (EL4), and F629 (TM10). The extracellular gate residues R216 and D633 engage in hydrogen bond and salt bridge interactions with both inhibitors (Fig. 4f, g), including a charged-reinforced hydrogen bond and a salt bridge between D633 and the R4 pendant ammoniums, and a hydrogen bond between the side chain of R216 and the carbonyl oxygen of R1. The allosteric pocket resembles that in MRS7292-bound DAT20, suggesting a common allosteric regulatory site in SLC6 transporters. However, this site is distinct from the vilazodone binding site in SERT22 (Supplementary Fig. 16).

MD-based r.m.s.d. analysis confirmed stable binding of ORG25543 to the allosteric site for 95.4% of combined simulation replicas. The central benzamide phenyl ring (R1) showed minimal fluctuation, due to stabilization by TM1b, EL4, and TM8 (Supplementary Fig. 17, 18, and Supplementary Table 4), however the distal benzyloxy phenyl (R2) and solvated pendant ammonium (R4) had greater mobility (Supplementary Fig. 19). R2 frequently interacted with its surrounding residues (Supplementary Table 4, Supplementary Fig. 18) and despite higher fluctuations, R3 remained in a hydrophobic cavity flanked by Y286 and Y287 on TM3 (Supplementary Fig. 19).

Hydrogen bond analysis indicated stable interactions between the benzamide of ORG25543 and L211 as well as intermittent interactions with R216. The protonated amine (R4) of ORG25543 intermittently engaged in a charged-reinforced hydrogen bond with D633, in agreement with our cryo-EM data (Supplementary Table 4, Supplementary Figs. 18, 19). The probability density map showing the relative likelihood of bound hGlyT2 ligand positions (Supplementary Fig. 19) demonstrated that ORG25543 remained in a deep energetic minimum at the allosteric binding site with an occupancy of 95%. In comparison, RPI-GLYT2-82, adopted a less stable binding pose than ORG25543, exhibiting higher positional fluctuations within the first 50 ns of simulations. It remained in the binding site for only 48% of the combined simulation replicas and moved towards the central vestibule of GlyT2 for the remaining time (Supplementary Fig. 19). Like ORG25543, the R2–R4 substituents of RPI-GLYT2-82 exhibited the greatest positional fluctuations, and the central indoline of R1 formed contacts with the same set of residues that coordinate ORG25543’s R1 moiety (Supplementary Table 4, and Supplementary Fig. 18, 19).

To analyse MD simulation trajectories of inhibitor-bound hGlyT2 complexes, we calculated the binding enthalpy over the first 50 ns of the replicate simulations, during which both inhibitors maintained their cryo-EM binding conformations in hGlyT2. This revealed the significant contribution of L211, W215, and D633 to ORG25543 binding and the 0.83–0.92-fold reduction in binding enthalpy for RPI-GLYT2-82 compared to ORG25543 (95% C.I.) (Supplementary Fig. 19). The per-residue energy decompositions further suggest the lower experimental IC50 for RPI-GLYT2-82 stems from an altered interaction enthalpy with L211, R216, and P543 (Supplementary Fig. 19). Together, these data show that both ORG25543 and RPI-GLYT2-82 occupy the same allosteric site, but that RPI-GLYT2-82 adopts a less stable binding pose.

To determine whether glycine can bind to inhibitor-bound hGlyT2 conformations obtained by cryo-EM, we first docked glycine into the inhibitor-bound structures and assessed the stability of the binding poses using MD simulations. The observed exchange of solvent and ions between the extracellular space and the substrate-binding site, together with glycine’s mobility within the substrate binding cavity, suggests that glycine can access the ORG25543- or RPI-GLYT2-82–bound hGlyT2Δ185 from the extracellular solvent. These findings support a mechanism in which allosteric inhibitors such as ORG25543 and RPI-GLYT2-82 inhibit glycine transport by preventing conformational cycling, a process independent of glycine binding (Supplementary Table 5, 6 and Supplementary Fig. 20).

RPI-GLYT2-82 binds reversibly to hGlyT2
Having characterized the allosteric pocket to which ORG25543 and RPI-GLYT2-82 bind, we sought to determine the features responsible for reversible binding of RPI-GLYT2-82. Likely due to the important role of W215 in accommodating the R1 and R2 substituents of both inhibitors, a conservative mutation to phenylalanine resulted in a detectable decrease in the potency of inhibition of transport by ORG25543 (~three-fold) and significant decrease in the potency of RPI-GLYT2-82 (IC50 > 30 μM) (Fig. 4j, l). Interestingly, although this W215F mutation had a relatively minor effect on potency, it significantly increased the rate of ORG25543 washout (Fig. 4k), similar to the effect of the mutation of the nearby Y550 (EL4) residue31. Likewise, mutation of the neighbouring D633 residue to glutamate significantly reduced the potency of inhibition for both ORG25543 (~14-fold) and RPI-GLYT2-82 (>18-fold) and accelerated ORG25543 washout (recovery from ORG25543 within five minutes), highlighting the critical role of this interaction for the potency of the inhibitors (Fig. 4j–l). Notably, washout of RPI-GLYT2-82 from both GlyT2W215F and GlyT2D633E was almost immediate, consistent with the reversible binding mode of the compound (Fig. 4m).

The pendant phenyl rings (R2) of both ORG25543 and RPI-GLYT2-82 snorkel deep into the binding pocket to engage in edge-to-face π-π interactions with W215 and Y550 (Fig. 4f, g). The R2 groups of both inhibitors are positioned orthogonally to their R1 core, however, as a benzamide, the pendant benzoyl phenyl ring of RPI-GLYT2-82 is likely to adopt a lower energy coplanar orientation with the carbonyl to which it is attached, reducing conformational flexibility. However, in its binding pose in the allosteric pocket, this RPI-GLYT2-82 pendant phenyl ring must twist nearly 90 degrees to adopt an orthogonal orientation, which likely induces torsional strain and is therefore energetically unfavourable52. The indoline benzamide carbonyl oxygen of RPI-GLYT2-82 also points toward a non-polar pocket (Fig. 4g), further contributing to destabilizing contacts. The R3 substituent of ORG25543 is a small hydrophobic cyclopentane ring that easily fits into a hydrophobic pocket in the binding site (Fig. 4f), potentially displacing any resident waters and interacting via van der Waals bonds. However, RPI-GLYT2-82 has a tetrahydropyran R3 substituent that is larger and more polar than the ORG25543 cyclopentane ring and its oxygen atom is not engaged in any significant binding interactions within the hydrophobic R3 pocket of the binding site (Fig. 4g). The increased size of this tetrahydropyran ring coupled with the lack of significant binding interactions with the polar tetrahydropyran oxygen may enable solvent water to “dissolve” the ring out of hydrophobic binding. Thus, the conformational inflexibility of R2, together with the larger and more polar R3 substituent, are likely responsible for the lower potency and improved washout kinetics of RPI-GLYT2-82 compared to ORG25543.

RPI-GLYT2-82 provides analgesia in mouse models of neuropathic pain
Although ORG25543 provided analgesia in animal models of neuropathic pain, it caused significant side effects that were likely due to its high affinity and slow dissociation rate28. To evaluate the in vivo utility of our reversible GlyT2 inhibitor RPI-GLYT2-82, we performed plasma and central nervous system pharmacokinetic (PK) profiling in mice and calculated unbound drug concentrations in plasma (Cu,p) and brain (Cu,b) at 30- and 120-minutes post-administration (Supplementary Note 1, and Supplementary Fig. 21, Supplementary Table 7, 9–13,). We initially selected a 50 mg/kg i.p. dose to obtain a preliminary PK readout and quantify unbound exposures in both compartments. Notably, this dose produced unbound brain concentrations that approximated the in vitro IC50 of RPI-GLYT2-82, indicating that it would likely afford sufficient target engagement and thus serve as a rational starting point for assessing analgesic efficacy (Supplementary Table 14–15). Indeed, RPI-GLYT2-82 achieved a Cu,b of 597.89 nM at 30 minutes after dosing (Fig. 1d, and Supplementary Table 7), approximately equal to its hGlyT2 IC50, supporting the expectation of achieving pharmacologically meaningful GlyT2 occupancy in vivo. Encouraged by these data, we tested RPI-GLYT2-82 in the CCI mouse models of neuropathic pain by measuring mechanical and cold allodynia in mice upon i.p. administration. When measuring mechanical allodynia, we observed dose-dependent anti-allodynia at both 50 and 100 mg/kg, with maximum efficacy between 90 min and 3 hours post-administration (Fig. 5a). This is comparable to the effect of 30 mg/kg ORG25543, which peaked between 1 and 2 hours post-administration28. Similarly, when measuring response by cold allodynia, peak anti-allodynia effects were observed within 2 hours at both 50 and 100 mg/kg with comparable efficacy to the control compound gabapentin (Fig. 5b). We further tested RPI-GLYT2-82 in the PSNL model by measuring its effects on mechanical allodynia and observed similar effects to the CCI model (Fig. 5c).

Although ORG25543 reversed mechanical allodynia at a dose of 50 mg/kg, this coincided with near-complete loss of rotarod performance, seizures and in one case, lethality28. A 50 mg/kg analgesic dose of RPI-GLYT2-82 was not associated with adverse neuromotor effects or muscle weakness (Fig. 5d–f), and did not change respiration frequency, minute volume (MVb), or tidal volume (TVb) measured by whole-body plethysmography (Fig. 5g–i). A supramaximal 250 mg/kg dose (i.p.), which is five-fold higher than the maximally analgesic dose of RPI-GLYT2-82, produced an initial 61% reduction in baseline rotarod performance, which was restored over the 90-minute time course, and caused transient muscle weakness 30 min post-injection which recovered at the 60-min time point (Fig. 5d, e). Whilst the grip strength and rotarod experiments show mild, transient deficits in muscle strength and motor coordination at the supramaximal analgesic dose, they do not coincide with the anti-allodynic effects. Given the temporal separation of these motor side-effects from the anti-allodynia effects, they do not pose a confound in interpreting the motor response-dependent pain-like behaviors. The supramaximal 250 mg/kg dose of RPI-GLYT2-82 also caused transient changes in respiratory frequency and MVb in the first hour, and TVb in the first 30 min (Fig. 5g–i). These effects coincided with transient sedation, which was most apparent in the first 15–30 minutes and fully recovered by 90 minutes (Fig. 5d–f).

These in vivo data provide evidence that RPI-GLYT2-82 produces statistically significant dose dependent analgesia without the adverse neuromotor effects associated with ORG2554328,33. Interestingly, although the primary target of RPI-GLYT2-82 is GlyT2 (IC50 = 554 nM, Fig. 1d), it is also a less potent antagonist at the serotonin 2A (5-HT2A) receptor (IC50 = 1.9 μM, Supplementary Note 1, Supplementary Fig. 22, 23). This additional activity may contribute to its suppression of pain signals. Indeed, antagonism of 5-HT2A has previously been reported for other ORG25543-based GlyT2 inhibitors, including opiranserin37,38. RPI-GLYT2-82 also exhibits appreciable inhibitory activity at SERT (IC50 = 4.7 μM, Supplementary Fig. 23), but has no significant binding activity at the dopamine (hDAT) or norepinephrine (hNET) transporters (10 μM RPI-GLYT2-82 displaces ~20% of 3H-1-[1-(2-benzo[b]thiopheneyl)cyclohexyl]piperidine hydrochloride (3H-BTCP) from hDAT and <5% of 3H-nisoxetine from hNET, Supplementary Note 1, Supplementary Fig. 22). Additionally, it is inactive at other off-target sites covered by our Cerep panels screen that are known to promote sedation (γ-aminobutyric acid type A (GABAA), histamine (H1), adenosine, adrenergic, and muscarinic receptors) (Supplementary Fig. 22, and Supplementary Table 16, 17). Finally, because the rewarding properties of opioids limit their use in the clinic, we compared RPI-GLYT2-82 and morphine in a conditioned place preference (CPP) paradigm. Mice treated with morphine (10 mg/kg, i.p.) exhibited a significant increase in preference for the paired chamber (p = 0.0287) whereas mice treated with RPI-GLYT2-82 (50 and 150 mg/kg, i.p.) showed no significant preference (p = 0.78 and p = 0.15, respectively) (Fig. 5j). Collectively, our data show that RPI-GLYT2−82 provides a foundation for the development of a non-addictive medication for neuropathic pain.
